Introducing Orbit, a smaller model for long documents

This post first appeared on the Example Lab blog and is republished here with permission.

Today we are releasing Orbit, a language model built to read long documents in one pass. Orbit accepts up to two million tokens of input, which is enough for a full legal contract bundle, a year of meeting notes or a large software repository, and it answers questions about that material with citations to the passages it used.

Orbit is smaller than our largest models. It has roughly forty billion parameters and runs on a single accelerator node, which keeps the cost of a long query close to the cost of a short one on earlier systems. We trained it on a mixture of public web text, licensed books and synthetic question and answer pairs written about long source documents.

On our internal long context benchmark Orbit finds the right passage in ninety one percent of questions, compared with seventy eight percent for the model it replaces. It is weaker at open ended creative writing, and we do not recommend it for that use. Like every model we release, Orbit can make mistakes, so answers about contracts, health or money should be checked by a person.

Orbit is available today to developers through the platform, with a free tier for research groups. Pricing is listed on the pricing page, and the model card describes the evaluations we ran, the data we used and the limits we know about. We will publish a technical report with full benchmark details next month.

We would like to thank the many teams who worked on Orbit, and the outside researchers who tested early versions and told us where it fell short.
